In his recent guest post on Noahpinion,
[Where's the "intelligence explosion"?](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/wheres-the-intelligence-explosion),
the futurologist Ramez Naam explains why he's skeptical about a runaway takeoff driven by recursive self-improvement,
sometimes called "FOOM"[^foom].

[^foom]: FOOM is not an acronym. It's the sound of a LOUD explosion.
    [Yudkowsky](https://youtube.com/watch?v=722LXkh5OGs&t=225s) popularized it, but it's
    [not clear who originated the term](https://www.reddit.com/r/singularity/comments/12bisxu/what_does_foom_stand_for_who_coined_this_term).

The post is worth reading in its entirety, but here's the nutshell. The frontier labs are spending an absolute
fortune[^rsi-investment] applying AI to the development of AI. Indeed, Anthropic claim that
[26% of their AI research is now led by AI](https://www.anthropic.com/institute/measuring-pace-of-ai-development).
Naam distinguishes five overlapping ways AI can improve AI, and argues, citing evidence from the labs themselves, that
all of them face "diminishing returns".

![Key infographic from the Naam post, which acknowledges that AI is speeding up AI development, but claims this somehow falls short of "fast takeoff"](/assets/images/rsi-chart.webp){#fig-naam}

[^rsi-investment]: We don't have good numbers here. In June, Claude Code's creator Boris Cherny said he'd
    [used over 8 billion tokens since March](https://app.dealroom.co/news/note/boris-cherny-on-coding-from-his-phone-and-the-post-coding-bottleneck).
    If a few thousand Anthropic engineers coded like that, it would cost hundreds of millions of dollars
    a year. But Cherny is hardly typical, and that's just coding assistance; automated experimentation
    probably costs far more. The ceiling is total compute: nearly
    $9B in the first half of 2026, [according to the WSJ](https://thenextweb.com/news/anthropic-s-1-750bn-compute-80-7bn-loss), most of it for training and serving models. Maybe $1B
    a year is a reasonable guess?

## The Maths Bit

Wisely, perhaps, Naam doesn't include a formula. But the underlying assumption is that the speed of **progress**
(scientific, economic, etc.[^social]) is linked to the current level of progress. The more progress we make, the faster
progress becomes. Because, roughly, we're building and improving tools all the time.

[^social]: We don't talk about social progress. The idea of social progress has the unmistakable whiff of socialism.
Indeed one might say the very idea of social progress is characteristic of socialism.

A simple mathematical model of this sort is that the speed with which progress, ahem, progresses (written
$\frac{dP}{dt}$) is proportional to the $k$-th power of the current level of progress ($P^k$).

$$
\frac{dP}{dt} \propto P^k
$$

This is a "differential equation" that characterizes the behaviour of the system. Solving it gives very different curves
depending on $k$. Everything depends on the value of $k$, which is something we can try to estimate from data.

Naam's evidence includes:

- At OpenAI, researchers used 124× more tokens per person and shipped about 7× as many lines of code, but ran only 1.6×
  as many experiments.
- At Anthropic, staff report a productivity uplift of around 4×. Naam reckons doubling the pace of progress would need
  about 40×.

He also draws on the returns to experiments in other sciences, on chess engines, and on a model of the feedback loop by
[Tom Cunningham and colleagues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15802). From all this he estimates that each extra point of
AI capability (on Epoch's ECI benchmark) buys 2–3% more research productivity. For the loop to sustain itself it would
need to be 15–19%. Very roughly, that puts $k$ at about 0.15: these are the "diminishing returns".

Nothing to worry about, see?

## Straw Man Singularity ($K\gt1$)

Well, no.

Start with $k>1$, the scariest regime. Suppose for the sake of argument that we're at progress level 0.1, and that
$k=2$. We can show that the progress at time $t$ is

$$
P(t) = \frac{1}{10 - t}
$$

So at time 10, the denominator goes to zero and progress goes to infinity.

Nothing real goes infinite, of course. A blow-up just tells you where the model stops working, and blow-up models can
fit the past beautifully right up until they don't. In 1960 Heinz von Foerster and colleagues
[fitted just such a curve](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.132.3436.1291) to two thousand years of world population.
Their ["Doomsday Equation"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinz_von_Foerster#Doomsday_equation) predicted 5.99 billion
people by 1997; the actual figure was 5.92 billion. Since then, population growth has fallen steadily behind the curve.

Hardly anyone takes the blow-up literally for progress either. Even the models that produce one treat it as the point
where the model breaks, not as a forecast. So if fast takeoff means $k>1$, as Naam's "accelerating returns" suggests,
it's a straw man.

## Self-Sustaining Singularity ($K\approx1$)

What people do believe is that $k$ is approximately 1. At $k=1$ progress is "exponential": progress, the rate of
progress, the rate of the rate of progress and so on all keep growing. None ever hits infinity, but wait long enough and
they are arbitrarily large. Ray Kurzweil, the most influential singularitarian[^coined], has spent his career here, or a
hair above[^double]. In
[The Law of Accelerating Returns](https://www.writingsbyraykurzweil.com/the-law-of-accelerating-returns) he spells out
what that means for the century we're in:

[^coined]: He didn't coin the term "singularity". That was John von Neumann, as
    [recalled by Stanislaw Ulam](https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1958-64-03/S0002-9904-1958-10189-5/S0002-9904-1958-10189-5.pdf)
    in 1958. But Kurzweil did the most to popularise it.

[^double]: Strictly, he argues for a "double" exponential, "meaning that the rate of exponential growth is itself
    growing exponentially". If $P = e^{e^t}$ then $\frac{dP}{dt} = P \ln P$: faster than $P^1$, slower than $P^k$ for
    any $k>1$, so it still never reaches infinity in finite time.

> it isn't the case that we'll experience 100 years of progress in the 21st century. Rather we'll witness on the order
> of twenty thousand years of progress — at today's rate of progress, that is.

Naam's 15–19% threshold tests exactly this: can the loop sustain itself? But it tests one narrow loop, AI making AI
software better, with everything else held fixed. He says so himself: "This model isolates the software loop; outside
investment can still drive rapid progress." On that loop his data say we're 5-10x short.

But no-one thinks the narrow loop runs alone. Kurzweil's accelerating returns span the whole technology stack, and
Google alone has used AI to
[speed up Gemini's training and tweak its TPU designs](https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/alphaevolve-a-gemini-powered-coding-agent-for-designing-advanced-algorithms/),
[cut the energy used to cool its data centres](https://green.googleblog.com/2016/07/deepmind-ai-reduces-energy-used-for.html)
and
[plan how to steer the plasma in a fusion reactor](https://www.ans.org/news/2025-10-22/article-7484/commonwealth-fusion-systems-partners-with-google-deepmind/).
These gains are small and slow; they show the wider loop exists, not how strong it is. Naam offers no estimate for it.
He's simply "not convinced" that fast takeoff "is possible under realistic conditions".

So the narrow loop gets a number and the loop we actually care about gets a shrug. Naam's "skeptical" headline misleads
readers by suggesting that the shortfall in the first somehow applies to the second.

He chose the narrow loop. It makes a serviceable noose.

## Subjective Singularity ($K<1$)

But let's suppose that the wide loop falls short too, and $k<1$. Here's the thing: that's not much less bonkers.
"Diminishing returns" doesn't mean slowing to a halt. Progress keeps growing forever, and so does its rate, just ever
more gently. And it only has to be fast enough to disorientate: if we start making mathematical breakthroughs every day,
it doesn't have to be every hour. That's a very strange world for primates who spent millennia figuring out how to use
twigs to catch ants.

Beyond a certain point, progress might as well be infinite for our dumb primate brains. Alvin Toffler had a name for
this back in 1970. "Future shock" is

> the shattering stress and disorientation that we induce in individuals by subjecting them to too much change in too
> short a time.

Some weeks it feels like we're there already.
